h: Ruins, a murder and Arthur's Seat
p: Holyroodhouse has one of the most dramatic stories in Scottish history. In 1566, Mary, Queen of Scots' private secretary, David Rizzio, was murdered in her chambers by a group of conspirators that included her own husband, Lord Darnley. You can see the rooms where it happened, and it's a gripping, grisly tale.

Make sure you head into the ruins of Holyrood Abbey, right beside the palace. The abbey was founded in 1128 by King David I, and its roofless nave, with tall arched windows open to the sky, is a beautiful, atmospheric spot. The palace gardens are lovely too when they're open.

Allow a couple of hours, and remember the palace can close when the royal family is in residence or for official events, so check before you go. The King's Gallery, near the palace entrance, shows exhibitions from the Royal Collection with its own tickets.

Right on the doorstep is Holyrood Park, with the dramatic hill of Arthur's Seat rising above it. Climbing to the top is a proper Edinburgh rite of passage, with fantastic views over the city and out to the Firth of Forth. Allow a good couple of hours for the walk, and wear sturdy shoes.

Opposite the palace is the striking modern Scottish Parliament building, and Dynamic Earth, a science centre that's a hit with kids, is close by. Then wander back up the Royal Mile through the Canongate, full of old closes, pubs and shops.
